cues.text: Let us turn now to chapter five: business model innovation and platform strategy.
We begin with a simple question.
When a company says it has a new business model, what exactly has changed?
A business model describes how an organisation creates, delivers and captures value.
Notice those three verbs: create, deliver, capture.
Creating value means producing something that is useful to someone.
Delivering value means getting it to them.
Capturing value means earning something in return, so that the organisation can sustain itself.
To make this concrete and complete, a widely used tool called the business model canvas breaks a business model into nine parts.
First, customer segments: the different groups of people or organisations the business serves.
Second, value propositions: the benefit or solution offered to each segment.
Third, channels: how the business reaches customers and delivers that value.
Fourth, relationships: the kind of connection maintained with customers, whether personal, automated or community-based.
Fifth, revenue streams: how money comes in.
Sixth, key resources: the important assets needed, such as people, technology, data or capital.
Seventh, key activities: the most important things the organisation must do.
Eighth, partners: the outside organisations that help it operate.
And ninth, cost structure: the main costs of running the model.
Hold those nine in mind, because we will keep returning to them.
Here is an important caution.
Technology may enable a new model without itself being the model.
A mobile app is not a business model.
The app is a tool.
The model is the answer to who the customers are, what value they receive, and how the organisation earns revenue and covers costs.
Technology can make a new answer possible, but it is not the answer.
Now let us look at common examples of revenue approaches.
Subscription means customers pay recurring access fees, for example monthly, to keep using a service.
Freemium means a basic version is free while a premium version is paid.
Transaction commissions mean the business takes a share each time a transaction occurs.
Advertising-supported services are offered to users, with advertisers providing the revenue.
Pay-per-use means customers pay according to how much they actually use.
And direct sales means the customer simply buys a product or service outright.
Next, the idea of a platform.
A platform facilitates exchanges or complementary innovation.
In other words, it either helps different parties trade with one another, or it provides a base on which other parties can build additional products and services.
A two-sided marketplace is a platform that connects buyers and sellers.
An ecosystem is broader.
It includes participants, complementary services, governance and infrastructure.
So think of the marketplace as the meeting place, and the ecosystem as the whole community around it, together with the rules and the foundations that keep it running.
This brings us to network effects.
Network effects occur when participation increases value for other users.
Each new participant makes the platform more useful to others.
There are two kinds.
Direct network effects arise within one group.
A messaging service is a classic illustration: each additional user makes it more valuable to the people already there, because there are more people to reach.
Indirect network effects arise across groups.
More sellers attract buyers, and more buyers attract sellers.
Each side draws in the other.
Be careful not to confuse this with economies of scale.
Economies of scale reduce average costs as volume grows.
That is about the cost per unit falling.
Network effects are about value to users rising as participation grows.
They are different ideas, even though both reward growth.
Network effects can also work against a platform.
Negative effects include congestion, spam, poor quality, fraud and unfair concentration.
More participants is not automatically better if the platform becomes crowded, filled with low-quality listings, or open to dishonest behaviour, or if power concentrates unfairly.
Now consider the difficulty every new marketplace faces: the chicken-and-egg problem.
Suppliers need buyers, and buyers need suppliers.
Who arrives first?
The source gives a sequence of responses.
Start with a narrow, high-value niche, so that you only need to build a small, meaningful community.
Recruit anchor participants, the important early members who give others a reason to join.
Reduce joining friction, so that signing up is easy.
Provide useful standalone tools, meaning features that are valuable to a participant even before the other side has arrived.
Build trust.
And carefully subsidise early participation, meaning you may support early users with incentives, but carefully.
Incentives should support real transactions, not fake sign-ups.
A thousand empty registrations are worth far less than a few genuine trades.
How do you know whether the platform is healthy?

Monitor four things: liquidity, which means successful matches; retention, which is whether participants keep coming back; acquisition costs, which is what it costs to win each participant; and contribution margin, which is what is left from revenue after the variable costs of each transaction.
Let us now work through the unit economics example, step by step, using naira.
The platform charges five per cent on a twenty thousand naira transaction.
Five per cent of twenty thousand naira is one thousand naira, so the platform earns one thousand naira.
Next, suppose payment processing and support cost four hundred naira.
Subtract four hundred from one thousand, and the contribution before fixed costs is six hundred naira.
Now suppose the acquisition cost is six thousand naira.
To recover it, divide six thousand by six hundred, which gives ten.
So about ten equivalent transactions are needed to recover the acquisition cost.
Remember the assumption: this holds only if these simplified values remain stable.
Real fees, costs and customer behaviour change.
One more distinction here.
Gross merchandise value, or GMV, is the total traded value, not platform revenue.
In our example, the twenty thousand naira is the traded value, which counts toward GMV, while the platform's revenue is only the one thousand naira commission.
A platform with very large GMV may still earn a small share of it.
Finally, governance.
Platform governance defines admission rules, quality standards, identity, payments, disputes, safety, data access and fair treatment.

These are the rules of the community: who may join, what standard is required, how people are verified, how money moves, how conflicts are settled, how people are kept safe, who can see which data, and how everyone is treated fairly.
APIs, or application programming interfaces, allow controlled integration.
They let outside developers and partners connect to the platform in an approved way.
But ecosystem openness must balance innovation against security and privacy.
The more open the platform, the more others can innovate, but the greater the exposure if safeguards are weak.
Lastly, competition.
Multi-homing allows participants to use competing platforms.
A seller might list on two marketplaces, or a driver might work for two services.
Switching costs and differentiation affect loyalty: when it is costly to leave, or when a platform offers something distinctive, participants are more likely to stay.
And remember the closing qualification: network effects do not guarantee monopoly or profit.
A platform can have strong network effects and still face competition, multi-homing, and unprofitable economics.

To summarise the logic of the chapter in one line: a business model is how value is created, delivered and captured; platforms add network effects and governance to that; and success depends on trust, healthy unit economics and careful balance between openness and control.
